items.title: The deal closed. When do the savings start?
items.description: Purchasing synergies can materially improve homebuilder acquisition savings and strengthen the economics of the deal. They can also be overstated when the deal model doesn't fully reflect the cost and time required to achieve them. Combining the purchasing volume of two builders should create leverage for better pricing and stronger margins. But before that leverage is real, someone has to determine what each company is buying, how their supplier agreements differ and what it will take to operate under a common set of processes. That's where the financial projections meet the realities of running the business. I've worked on acquisition diligence and integration across different industries, and the question I believe deserves more attention isn't how much a deal can save. It's when those savings actually show up in the P&L. For homebuilders , technology has a significant role in the solution. Buying power only matters if you can use it Consider a builder acquiring a regional operation with established supplier relationships and a healthy pipeline of homes under construction . The opportunity is clear. The combined company is buying more materials across more communities, which should create leverage to negotiate better terms. Now look at what has to happen to capture those savings. The acquired company may use a different ERP, organize its purchasing data differently or have supplier agreements that don't align with the parent company's contracts. Before purchasing leadership can negotiate from a position of combined volume, they need an accurate, combined view of what that volume actually is. Meanwhile, both businesses still have homes to build. Construction schedules can't be put on hold while systems are reconciled. It's entirely possible to have a sound purchasing strategy and spend the first several months after closing working through the operational issues that prevent successful execution. As builders know better than anyone, these delays carry real cost. If the acquisition model assumes purchasing savings will start contributing to margin within two quarters and integration takes a year, you won't get the return you underwrote. The savings may still arrive, but every quarter of delay is value that doesn't come back. This matters even more when interest rates are high. There's usually a second cost hiding in the same delay: running two sets of systems, two sets of processes and often two teams doing the same work until integration is complete. Those dual running costs rarely get the same scrutiny as the synergy number. Homebuilder M&A integration is a financial decision Technology deserves a more prominent place in acquisition diligence and homebuilder M&A integration, particularly when operating efficiencies account for a meaningful share of the expected return. Knowing which applications a company runs is a starting point. The more important question is how those systems will work inside the larger organization, and what it will cost to get them there. Can the acquiring builder get reliable purchasing data across both businesses on day one? Can existing systems exchange the information needed to keep construction moving? What will it cost to maintain separate environments while integration is underway, and for how long? These sound like operating questions. They're also valuation questions. The same applies to proprietary technology . Many builders have invested heavily in systems developed specifically for their businesses, and there can be good reasons for doing so. The challenge arises when those systems must accommodate an organization they weren't originally designed to support. Custom integrations require people and capital to build. They also require ongoing security and maintenance as the business changes, and that cost doesn't end when the integration goes live. I want to understand those costs before committing to an acquisition, not discover them in the first integration budget review. The advantage of an established network One factor that is often overlooked in technology discussions is the value of connectivity that already exists. A homebuilding operation depends on relationships with suppliers, manufacturers and trades that extend well beyond its internal systems. Those connections become particularly important when a company expands into new markets or brings another Builder into the organization. At Hyphen Solutions, we've spent more than 25 years building a network that connects hundreds of Builders and more than 18,000 suppliers, trades and manufacturers across North America. That matters because a builder operating within an established network isn't starting from zero. In many acquisitions, the acquired builder's suppliers are already on the same network as the parent company. When that's the case, many of the connections the combined company needs exist before the deal closes, and purchasing teams aren't onboarding suppliers a second time while homes are under construction. Our technology connects construction scheduling, purchasing and supplier communication, and integrates with different ERP and back-office environments. That gives purchasing leadership the combined view of orders, pricing and supplier activity across both businesses that consolidated buying depends on, without replacing every existing system first. We’ve seen this play out over the past year as a number of builders combined operations, and the ones that moved fastest had something in common. Their companies already shared many of the same suppliers and trades on the Hyphen network. Bringing everyone onto a single instance went quicker, and the trades doing the work in the field had a much simpler transition. Nobody was asking a framer to learn a new system in the middle of a build. There will still be work to do following an acquisition. items.title: The mortgage operating model after AI
items.description: In my previous two articles, I explored why the mortgage industry's biggest AI challenge is structural and how the traditional brokerage operating model creates complexity as businesses grow . That brings us to a more fundamental question: If we could redesign mortgage origination around what AI now makes possible, what would we build? Today, the process is organized around a series of narrowly defined roles and handoffs, with loan officers, assistants, processors, underwriters and others each responsible for moving the file to the next stage. Every handoff creates another opportunity for information to get lost and responsibility to be pushed downstream. I believe the mortgage operating model of the future will be organized around a persistent, provable understanding of the borrower and the lifecycle of the loan, rather than the people, systems and handoffs that define the process today. Start with an evidence-based picture of the borrower At its core, a mortgage involves building an evidence-based profile of an individual and applying a risk model to it. Today, that profile is repeatedly reconstructed or revalidated by originators, lenders, underwriters and other participants because each has limited visibility into, or confidence in, the work that came before. Imagine instead a persistent, evidence-backed borrower profile that brings together information from pay stubs, tax returns, credit reports and other sources, with each data point retaining a verifiable connection to its original evidence. That includes where the information came from and how it was calculated, interpreted or reconciled with other information. The result would be a more complete and transparent understanding of the borrower that persists throughout the loan lifecycle. Rather than reconstructing that information each time another party needs to assess the loan, participants could trace the underlying evidence, understand how previous conclusions were reached and build on the work already performed, while still conducting their own necessary evaluations and verifications. Apply different risk models to the same underlying evidence To be sure, understanding the borrower is only part of the equation. Every lender, agency and mortgage product has its own requirements and risk criteria. Today, those requirements are translated into guidelines, matrices and documents that must be interpreted and applied by people across multiple stages of the origination process. With a common, verifiable borrower profile, different risk models could be applied to the same underlying information. A system could evaluate how Fannie Mae , Freddie Mac or a particular lender would assess the borrower, identify missing evidence and determine what needs to happen next. Specialized AI agents could then coordinate and execute much of that work, from collecting documents and preparing calculations to addressing conditions and identifying exceptions that require human review. Consider how often a missing document or unresolved discrepancy surfaces late in the process, forcing a loan officer or processor to revisit work that should have been completed weeks earlier. With a more complete understanding of the borrower and the requirements of the loan, those agents could identify many of those issues earlier, coordinate the necessary follow-up and maintain an auditable record of the work performed. The implications extend beyond making individual tasks faster to changing how information is maintained and how work gets done, creating an opportunity to rethink the organization itself. When the loan carries the context, the organization can change When technology maintains the evidence, context and requirements throughout the loan lifecycle, people no longer need to serve as the connective tissue between every task and system. Specialized AI agents can increasingly handle work traditionally distributed across different roles, while experienced mortgage professionals oversee execution, validate results and exercise judgment. Consider the processor, whose role could evolve from coordinating documents, conditions and handoffs to overseeing the quality and performance of the loan process. Specialized AI agents could collect documents, prepare calculations and track conditions, while the processor sets standards, validates results, resolves exceptions and continuously improves the workflow. This shift would also change how mortgage organizations define and reward expertise. Rather than measuring success by the number of people someone manages or the tasks they complete, organizations could focus on accurate files, predictable closings, borrower experience and ultimately, a lower cost to originate. By reducing manual handoffs and repetitive work, experienced professionals could oversee more loans without a corresponding increase in staffing. The result would be a mortgage organization structured around the lifecycle of the loan rather than inherited job descriptions. Instead of scaling by adding more people to manage each stage of origination, companies could build teams around broader accountability for the loan from application to funding, with AI supporting the work required along the way. What it all means Origination is the logical place to prove this model because it is where the borrower's evidence is first assembled and evaluated. But once a provable, evidence-based profile exists, its usefulness could extend well beyond funding. Other participants across the mortgage value chain, including investors and capital markets firms, could eventually apply their own risk models to the same underlying information, allowing for more granular risk assessment without repeatedly reconstructing the loan. My prediction is that AI will reshape not only mortgage organizations , but also how they work together. items.title: Finance of America grows origination volume but reports $110M loss in Q3
items.description: Finance of America ( FOA ) reported a net loss of $110 million in the third quarter of 2026, as noncash fair value adjustments weighed on results despite growth in the company's home equity lending business. The Plano, Texas-based company on Tuesday reported $748 million in funded volume for the quarter ending Sept. 30, up 24% from $603 million during the same period last year. Year-to-date funded volume reached $2.07 billion, a 17% increase from the first nine months of 2025. FOA recorded a basic loss of $5.24 per share, compared with a loss of 98 cents per share in the third quarter of 2025. The quarterly net loss was primarily driven by $125 million in noncash fair value adjustments. On an adjusted basis, FOA reported net income of $6 million, or 28 cents per share, compared with $33 million, or $1.33 per share, a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA totaled $17 million, down from $55 million in the third quarter of 2025. “The third quarter of 2026 demonstrated the continued strength of our platform, with funded origination volume growing 24% year over year. While higher interest rates drove near-term pressure on earnings , we believe this impact is temporary,” CEO Graham Fleming said in a statement. “We have already taken steps to improve margins.” During the company's earnings call, Fleming said the company remains focused on production growth, operational efficiency and cash generation, and explained that margins compressed after the Federal Reserve shifted from cutting to raising interest rates. "We have already made the necessary changes to product pricing, and we expect margins to return to historical levels in the first half of 2027," Fleming told investors. "Finance of America has grown volumes on average by 20% each year since 2023. The third quarter was a challenging rate environment, with the 10-year Treasury yields increasing over 75 basis points during the quarter, a reaction to the Fed's pivot to raising rates and elevated inflation," he added. Retirement solutions performance FOA’s retirement solutions segment, which originates home equity-based financing products, including reverse mortgages , recorded $748 million in funded volume during the quarter, up 24% year over year. "Our retirement solutions revenue margin was impacted in the third quarter, decreasing to 9%, compared with 11.3% in the third quarter of 2025, and a historical average since the start of 2024 of 10.7%," Fleming said during the call. "We believe these impacts are temporary and do not change the underlying fundamentals of our business." Revenue for the segment totaled $67 million, down 1% from the prior-year period and a decrease from Q2 2026 's $74 million. Pretax income fell to $3 million, down from $10 million a year earlier, while adjusted net income declined to $9 million, down from $20 million. The company attributed the decline in profitability primarily to pressure on origination margins as benchmark interest rates increased during the quarter. It said it implemented product and pricing adjustments to address the impact and expects margins to return to historical levels. For the first nine months of 2026, the retirement solutions segment generated $2.07 billion in funded volume, up 17% year over year. Revenue increased 14% to $208 million. "Since 2023, our submission volumes have increased by 21% annually, while our funded volume has grown by 20% annually. This is across our product suite, as HECM volume is up 14% year over year, HomeSafe first liens are up 15%, and HomeSafe seconds are up 63%," FOA President Kristen Sieffert said during the call. Portfolio management performance FOA's portfolio management segment, which generates revenue through net interest income and fair value changes on portfolio assets, reported a pretax loss of $138 million, compared with an $11 million loss in the third quarter of 2025. The company attributed the loss primarily to negative non-cash fair value adjustments on retained interests in securitizations. Portfolio management reported adjusted net income of $11 million, down from $30 million a year earlier. Assets under management in the segment increased 23% year over year to $37.4 billion. The growth reflected new originations and the acquisition of Onity Mortgage Corp. ‘s HECM servicing portfolio on July 1. For the first nine months of 2026, portfolio management recorded a pretax loss of $128 million, compared with pretax income of $202 million in the same period last year. Adjusted net income totaled $57 million, down from $66 million. FOA ended the third quarter with $118 million in cash and cash equivalents, up from $85 million at the end of June. The company attributed the increase to cash generation from originations and capital markets activity. Total equity stood at $307 million as of Sept. 30, including $259 million attributable to common stock. Book value was $28.08 per common share. The company said it expects to complete a $60 million paydown of senior secured notes in November. Looking ahead to the final quarter of 2026, chief financial officer Matt Engel said the company expects funded volume to reach $3.1 billion to $3.4 billion, a range "supported by consumer demographics , our product breadth, and ongoing conversion improvements." items.title: MSRs trade at richest levels in decades as lenders, funds pile in
items.description: Chicago-based Rate has recently changed its servicing strategy, retaining mortgage servicing rights ( MSRs ) instead of selling. “We've been retaining all of our MSRs for the last 12 months, so we're over $50 billion in MSR retention,” CEO Victor Ciardelli said in an exclusive interview with HousingWire . “We really believe in retaining the MSRs, staying close to the customer.” Rate’s approach reflects a broader trend of mortgage lenders holding onto their portfolios or seeking to add MSRs as a way to recapture borrowers when rates eventually fall. John Sullivan, managing director of MSR advisory services at Milliman , has seen that shift firsthand. Speaking during IMN’s Mortgage Servicing Rights Conference in New York on Monday, he said he’s having more conversations with clients about retaining their portfolios “unless liquidity is an issue,” and about monetizing them if they are not hedging . Higher demand for MSRs is not limited to independent mortgage banks ( IMBs ). Depository institutions are also showing more interest, executives told HousingWire during the conference. “ Banks historically are not great at recapture, but we think that given some changes on the Basel capital front, we're going to see more bank participation in this space on a go-forward basis, and I think banks will think about just customer acquisition in general, cross-selling in general,” said Larry Goldstone, president of capital markets and lending at BSI Financial Services . Strategic investors are also willing to grow their portfolios. Rob Williams, co-founder and CEO at Grander Investment Management , a specialized asset manager focused on MSRs, said he’s tactical but sees MSRs as a “spectacular asset” that can reach double-digit returns. “I can probably be more patient,” he said during the conference, when comparing his approach to the other buyers. “I can be more tactical.” The buyer base views MSRs through different lenses. Rich McRedmond, managing director at CrossCountry Mortgage , said that while banks see MSRs as part of their consumer banking strategy, real estate investment trusts ( REITs ) see them as a pure investment. And mortgage companies see them as a borrower recapture tool “from when they get the mortgage to when they get the next mortgage.” Multiples and yields Conventional, pristine MSRs are seeing 7x multiples amid high demand, a level not reached in more than two decades. “We've seen some pretty extraordinary multiples of late,” Goldstone said. “This is usually an inexpensive asset, and therefore an asset that people want to be able to own. I think you could hedge MSR pretty effectively and still get low-double digits, high-single digit returns up until about the last year. That's pretty attractive for an asset that really doesn't have a whole lot of credit risk associated with it.” Simon Aldrich, senior executive vice president at Freedom Mortgage , believes that at this point, “it’s very difficult to be in this market if you don’t have recapture.” “In our model, we don't hedge, so I'm not worried about rates going up or rates going down. Rates go up, I get the pickup at slower speeds. Rates go down, our call center kicks into gear.” Bayview Asset Management , which acquires MSRs from the bulk and flow markets and uses five different subservicers, has also built out a full recapture strategy, including through its acquisition of Guild Mortgage . Managing director Michael Lau said Bayview has partnered with investors, including sovereign wealth funds and pension funds, that have long-duration strategies. “MSRs are great because they're not correlated to the equity or the bond market , and gives them something alternative that also, because we hedge out all the interest rate risk for them, delivers a very consistent return on their money, net of our fees,” Lau said. Opportunistic sales Some companies have taken advantage of current pricing to sell MSRs for different reasons, including to pay back debt or raise funds. In the third quarter , Rocket Companies sold $23 billion of unpaid principal balance (UPB) for $379 million in cash proceeds, retaining the subservicing and recapture services on nearly 70% of the MSRs sold. Analysts told HousingWire the company usually sells production in the wholesale channel due to lower recapture possibility. Pennymac Financial Services entered into an agreement to sell $29 billion in UPB of low-coupon conventional MSRs, with $490 million of proceeds expected to pay down debt. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter. Meanwhile United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) sold about $60 billion — at a roughly 6x multiple — to JPMorgan Chase , sources told HousingWire. The companies declined to comment. This is part of a plan to bring up to $80 billion of MSRs to market in the fourth quarter, with the expectation of being paid more than $1.8 billion in an attempt to reduce leverage. Newrez President Baron Silverstein said his company is taking a disciplined approach. Across the Newrez portfolio, 60% of loans were originated before or during the COVID-19 pandemic. “In today's market, given where we are from a rate perspective, there's pressure in a competitive environment where MSRs get created — where that gain on sale is from an all-in gain-on-sale perspective on loans that we originate or buy. And when we think about that, we get very selective and stay very disciplined about how we put that capital to work,” Silverstein said. “When you think about hedging in a market like this, that also requires a lot of capital, and it's very challenging in these markets today, regardless of the interest rate environment. This has been the case for the last year to year and a half.” What's next? Looking ahead, servicing executives believe that multiples can stay higher as elevated mortgage rates reduce prepayment risks, which supports MSR cash flows. items.title: Texas Flips Blue, Putting Data Center Boom On Notice
items.description: Texas elected Democrats to its top offices for the first time in decades, a move that could ripple through the burgeoning data center industry across the state. X/Gina Hinojosa Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico Gina Hinojosa was named the projected winner for Texas governor, and James Talarico was named the projected winner for U.S. Senate on Tuesday night by The Associated Press. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott , the 12-year Republican incumbent, said he called Hinojosa to concede at about 10 p.m. CT Tuesday. Hinojosa had more than 4.4 million votes , or 53%, with 80% of Texas counties reporting late Tuesday, compared to about 3.8 million votes for Abbott. The 52-year-old Austin state representative overcame a 4-1 spending disparity and will become the first Latina governor of Texas. The Texas Republican Party hadn’t lost a gubernatorial election since 1990. For the Texas commercial real estate industry, all eyes will likely turn to Hinojosa’s plan for a data center development moratorium , as well as stricter regulations on water and power usage and an end to tax breaks for the industry. Texas has more data centers under development than any other state, and it rose in the ranks to the top data center market this year, surpassing Virginia. Talarico has also called for tighter data center regulations and said their construction shouldn’t contribute to the state’s affordability crisis . While the Republican candidates had also called for the end of tax breaks and stricter regulations for data center development, their plans differed at the granular level. Talarico’s defeat of the Republican Senate nominee, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton , will make him the state’s first Democratic senator since 1988, before the 37-year-old Talarico was born. Talarico had 4.7 million votes , or about 55%, to Paxton’s 3.7 million late Tuesday night. Paxton, who defeated incumbent John Cornyn in the primary election, faced controversies like his 2023 impeachment and high-profile members of his party refusing to back him . More than a third of the impeachment articles involved Paxton’s relationship with embattled Austin real estate developer Nate Paul . Paxton also has a significant real estate portfolio that is at issue in his ongoing divorce. items.title: Hynes Vows To Bring Property Tax Stability As New Cook County Assessor
items.description: The 2026 Illinois midterms featured a slew of Democratic wins across the ballot as part of sweeping victories for the party across the country. In perhaps the most consequential result for Illinois' commercial real estate investors, Democrat Pat Hynes handily won the race for Cook County assessor , defeating Libertarian challenger Nico Tsatsoulis by a margin of about 85% to 15%. Courtesy of Pat Hynes Pat Hynes Hynes, who unseated two-term incumbent Fritz Kaegi in the March Democratic primary, has promised to make the Assessor's Office "boring again" by being more predictable and accurate. The former Lyons Township assessor plans to create a new department in the Assessor's Office called the Department of Economic Development, which will work with aldermen and mayors to offer transparency in the assessment process for new development. Hynes is the second member of his family to lead the Assessor's Office. His uncle Thomas Hynes held the role from 1979 to 1997. Siegel Jennings partner Molly Phelan told Bisnow on Tuesday that she believes Hynes' win will bring more tax certainty to Cook County — and investors in tow. "I'm very bullish on development in Cook County because we're going to have a new assessor coming in," Phelan said. "I think we're going to have government that understands that we need more taxpayers and more buildings coming in to level out the property tax base." Elsewhere in Illinois, incumbent Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker comfortably secured a third term, capturing about 60% of the vote and defeating Republican challenger Darren Bailey and independent opponent Collin Corbett . Pritzker has been a major backer of the sprawling Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park on the South Side but has taken a more cautious approach to data center development in the state in 2026. Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton made history in her U.S. Senate win, as she will become the sixth Black woman to ever serve in the Senate. Alexi Giannoulias, who is a front-runner in the 2027 Chicago mayoral election, also won his campaign for secretary of state by a margin of 64% to 35%. items.title: Donalds Makes History With Win For Florida Governor, Voters OK Property Tax Amendment
items.description: Florida voters showed up — even as some poll locations were moved due to severe flooding — to elect Byron Donalds as the state’s 47th governor, succeeding Gov. Ron Desantis . Donalds makes history as the Sunshine State's first Black governor. In addition to electing the state’s first new governor in seven years, voters passed a property tax amendment that increases homestead exemptions significantly over the next two years. Bisnow/Chloe Gallivan Donalds won with 50.1% of the vote, a 1.4-percentage-point lead over his opponent, Democrat David Jolly . “As your next governor, we are going to make sure that Florida remains the very best state in all of America,” Donalds said at his watch party at Broward County’s Seminole Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Hollywood. “We're going to be focused on the issues that I've been talking about on this campaign trail for a long time. We are going to drive down costs for the people of this state.” Both candidates and their campaigns leaned heavily on their approaches to affordability, a leading issue for Florida, which is experiencing an outflow of middle-class residents citing affordability concerns. The trend is especially evident in South Florida, where an affordable housing crisis is brewing amid an influx of wealthy individuals. Miami-Dade County lost more than 10,000 residents between 2024 and 2025, placing it among the three counties with the nation’s largest population declines, according to the Census Bureau . Donalds, who has spent the last 10 years in Florida politics and serves as the U.S. representative for Florida’s 19th Congressional District, wants to lower homebuilding costs to boost housing inventory. He has called for smaller units from developers, removing zoning restraints, specifically in Miami-Dade County, and promoted the removal of local zoning restraints to boost housing inventory. The new governor-elect, a Florida State University graduate, also supports the state seeking technology to modernize permitting systems. In addition to a focus on affordability, Donalds pushed to expand transparency on healthcare costs and government spending, worked to move NASA’s headquarters and the Space Force Academy to Florida, and focused on early literacy for children. Jolly, a lawyer and former Republican congressman who turned Democrat in 2025, launched his run in June 2025, campaigning on affordability largely through property insurance, calling for state-backed funding to cover hurricane and wind risk with aims to cut premiums by up to 70%. He also supported using state money to invest in workforce and affordable housing and expanding down payment assistance. “The movement we started doesn't go away tomorrow,” Jolly said onstage at the Tampa Convention Center, where he held his watch party. “It exists to hold our leaders accountable.” Donalds’ win keeps Florida’s 28-year red streak alive, even after high expectations for Jolly’s performance, and falls in line with the real estate industry’s preferences . Wikimedia Commons/Gage Skidmore Byron Donalds at AmericaFest 2025 Some of South Florida’s largest commercial real estate investors funneled millions into Donalds’ campaign in recent months. It had amassed more than $150M by Tuesday, according to the Florida Department of State’s campaign finance database . That is a massive lead against the roughly $14M Jolly collected in donations by Election Day. Among the largest donors to Donalds were Citadel founder Ken Griffin , who donated $15M in two separate payments in July and August, and Related Ross head Stephen Ross , who donated $1M, according to the database. Other donors included Related Group , JDS Development ’s Michael Stern , Oak Row Equities and Property Markets Group . Jolly’s campaign landed donations from Compass agent Michelle Howland and Deborah Simon, daughter of Simon Property Group co-founder Melvin Simon. Florida’s new governor will be sworn into office in January. On top of heavy real estate backing, Donalds earned an almost immediate endorsement from President Donald Trump when he announced he was running for governor in February 2025 and later landed DeSantis’ backing . Beyond electing a new governor, voters approved a property tax amendment targeting housing costs, clearing the 60% hurdle to pass. The amendment will raise Florida’s $50K homestead exemption to $150K next year and $250K in 2028 without exempting tax levies for school district properties. Despite touting greater affordability for homeowners, localities have warned that the amendment’s passage could mean multimillion-dollar cuts to their budgets. In response to the measure, the city of Miami prepared a 25% budget cut to local hospitals, police, fire, parks, public schools and water management, which Related Group's Jorge Peréz cautioned could stunt the city’s ability to attract and retain residents. Landlords may carry the weight if municipalities opt to raise taxes on commercial properties to fund the gap. Rental properties that aren’t homesteaded, because they aren’t owner-occupied, could see a rise in property taxes, which could be passed on to renters . “Anytime some commercial businesses get their costs raised, they tend to pass it on to the consumer,” Kaufman Rossin tax principal and leader Ken Rios said. “So talking about affordability for the rental market, if the commercial owners are paying more, they may increase rents and it may impact the consumer.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Byron Donalds , David Jolly , Ron DeSantis

items.title: Developer Picks Up Industrial Site, Plots 1.3M SF Development: The Chicago Deal Sheet
items.description: Logistics Property Co. is making another Midwestern buy, picking up its fourth development site in the Chicago area in the last year. The company closed on a 74-acre site at 23960 S. Houbolt Road in Joliet for an undisclosed price. When the development is complete, the property will total close to 1.3M SF. Unsplash/user user “23960 S Houbolt Road is the premier location for bulk users given the immediate proximity to the intermodal and the new Houbolt Road Extension,” Ben Fish, associate market leader at the company, said in a statement. “We’re excited to continue to grow our Midwest portfolio with this property, our fourth development site in the Chicago market in the last year.” Acquisition of the development site follows the closing of three development properties: 424 Howard Ave. in Des Plaines, 390 O’Hare Logistics Park in Schaumburg, and 2349 W. Lake St. in Addison. Construction on the speculative building will start in the spring, and the project is expected to deliver the following spring, the company said in a release. Logistics Property Co.'s Fish and Vince Pergande worked with Cushman & Wakefield’s Ryan Klink on the deal. PEOPLE W.E. O’Neil Construction appointed Nicholas Schubert as general counsel. He will lead W.E. O’Neil’s enterprise legal and risk function, providing strategic and practical counsel on business and construction matters. He will also work with the company’s safety leadership to continue to incorporate safety into its approach to enterprise risk management. SALES An undisclosed buyer acquired a nearly 80K SF industrial facility at Exchange Avenue in Aurora from a private entity. The buyer plans to use the facility to support the expansion of its U.S. operations. Newmark's Corey Chase arranged the deal. *** W. P. Carey acquired the British International School of Chicago in a $70.6M deal, picking up the building from EPR Properties. The 102K SF property was completed in 2015 at 161 W. Ninth St. in the South Loop. Colliers’ Todd Noel, Mindy Korth, Kyle Campbell, David Burden, Josh McGee, Austin Little, Christian Rahe and Jack Johnson brokered the deal. *** NW1 Partners paid about $74M for a portfolio of eight truck parking and outdoor storage sites in the Chicago area, according to The Real Deal . The company acquired the sites from Transport Properties. The largest site was a 29.5-acre yard at 3000 E. 106th St. *** An unnamed investor acquired 1910-1912 Division St., an 18-unit multifamily property in Melrose Park. At the time of the sale, the property was 100% occupied, and units feature remodeled kitchens and baths. Essex Realty Group's Karla Galva represented the seller and buyer. LEASES Sampa USA signed a 62K SF industrial lease for its Midwest distribution hub at 2305 Kenyon Road in Bartlett. The facility is part of the three-unit Blue Heron 160 business park. Brown Commercial Group's Dan Brown represented the developer and owner, Cratos Industrial. *** Year Up United signed a roughly 13K SF lease at Two Prudential Plaza, with move-in slated by the end of this year. The East Loop location will establish the company's physical presence in Chicago. Savills' Brett Tynes and Brandon Nasatir advised Year Up United. *** Croke Fairchild Duarte & Beres and Point of Difference Strategies completed a 40K SF move to 222 N. LaSalle St. The firms’ new office brings their Chicago team together in one location and nearly doubles their footprint in the city. *** Whole Foods inked a 10K SF lease in Logan Square, aiming to open a small-format store in the neighborhood, Crain's Chicago Business reported . The company plans to open a Whole Foods Market Daily Shop at 2280 N. Milwaukee Ave. with a smaller footprint than its standard stores. The site was formerly home to Family Dollar. The community at 2506 N. Mannheim Road was developed by Evergreen Real Estate Group. F.H. Paschen managed construction, and Weese Langley Klein Architects designed the project. items.title: This 83-Acre Blue Ridge Mountain Wedding Estate Is Heading to Auction With No Reserve
items.description: Imagine hosting a wedding or lavish event for 150 friends and family right on your very own Blue Ridge Mountain farm. That could become a reality as an 83.56-acre property with a 5,000-square-foot event barn in Franklin, NC , heads to auction with no reserve on Nov. 7. Created in 2010, Tessentee Farm has multiple structures, including an eight-bedroom primary residence, three two-bedroom guest cabins, and plenty of space to entertain. "It has a nice big spread of land, so the duality of it also being an income-generating asset is pretty impressive," says Trayor Lesnock , founder and president of Platinum Luxury Auctions , who will host the auction. The listing is held by Isaiah Thomas Johns of Mountain Pro Real Estate Professionals . Loading... The primary residence has arched doorways, built-ins, French doors, and a dining room designed for hosting. Austin Marvel, Real Estate Photographer Loading... The rustic barn has exposed beams, wood-clad walls, string lighting, and an open field ideal for photos. Austin Marvel, Real Estate Photographer Loading... The chef's kitchen comes with a breakfast bar. Austin Marvel, Real Estate Photographer The property last changed hands for $2,500,000 in 2013 and had hit the market for $6.9 million in November 2025. “You have this large house with all the bells and whistles where you could live, an event barn, and three separate cabins where you could host events,” Lesnock says. “There is a good record of the farm being used for weddings and events.” The luxury event barn , which can be heated and cooled, has hosted everything from destination weddings and rehearsal dinners to milestone celebrations and corporate retreats. “We have had large families from the Blue Ridge Mountain region look at it and are wanting to use it for multigenerational living,” he notes. “About 50% were looking to use it as a private property and the other 50% were looking at it for the income generation.” Loading... The farm has multiple structures, including three two-bedroom guest cabins. Austin Marvel, Real Estate Photographer Loading... The spacious primary suite with fireplace Austin Marvel, Real Estate Photographer Loading... The pool has a water slide and a swim-up bar. Austin Marvel, Real Estate Photographer The primary residence has arched doorways, built-ins, French doors, a spacious dining room, a chef's kitchen with a breakfast bar, and a primary suite with a fireplace, soaking tub, and walk-in shower. Covered terraces overlook the pool, which has a water slide and a swim-up bar, as well as an outdoor kitchen and a hot tub. “It will probably go to someone who wants to use it privately,” Lesnock adds. “There are no outright restrictions, so you could develop it further.” The rustic barn has exposed beams, wood-paneled walls, string lighting, and an open field ideal for photos. A ceremony could be held in the pasture, followed by cocktails under the stars, and dinner and dancing inside the barn, with guests retreating to cabins for an overnight stay. Lesnock says the countryside setting could lend itself to an equestrian estate. “You could make it more of a farm and add an arena if you wanted,” he says. “Franklin is not an area that pops up on a lot of people’s maps, but it’s in the southern foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains. Asheville is only an hour away. There is also a creek that borders the property that is excellent for trout fishing.” Get real estate news in your inbox Sign up now Kellie Speed is a contributor to Realtor.com. As a writer and editor, she has worked for a variety of online and print publications, including Inked magazine, Jetset, Westchester magazine, JustLuxe, The Boston Globe, and U.S. Veterans Magazine. items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Food Network Star Alex Guarnaschelli Reveals Her Secrets To Turning Any Home Into a Holiday Entertaining Hub
items.description: Turning your home into a welcoming holiday gathering spot doesn’t have to mean buying new decorations or finding room for a formal dining setup. For Alex Guarnaschelli , a few thoughtful touches—and some planning before the doorbell rings—can help hosts make the most of their space and enjoy the celebration themselves. In an exclusive interview with Realtor.com® , the celebrity chef shared her advice for entertaining on a budget, organizing a busy kitchen, and keeping guests comfortable in smaller homes. “I always think a welcoming home is about the little details, not how much money you spend," she said. Her first suggestion is to adjust the lighting before guests arrive. "A few candles or lamps instead of bright overhead lighting can completely change the feeling of a room," she explained. When it comes to decorations, Guarnaschelli recommends looking for items that can serve another purpose once the party ends. Loading... Turning your home into a welcoming holiday gathering spot doesn’t have to mean buying new decorations or finding room for a formal dining setup. HSN “Second, bring something natural into the space," she said. "I love the idea of filling a bowl with beautiful oranges, pomegranates, or even fresh herbs from the grocery store. They're inexpensive, they look festive, and you can actually use them afterward.” Making guests comfortable from the moment they enter is another priority. “And third, think about what your guests experience when they arrive. Have a place for coats and bags, put on some music, and make sure there's something to eat or drink right away,” she advised. “You don't need a house that looks like a magazine. You just want people to walk in and feel like they're in the right place.” That thoughtful approach extends to the kitchen, where Guarnaschelli starts by considering how each dish fits into the cooking schedule. “I like to think of my kitchen almost like a restaurant kitchen before service. Everything should have a purpose and a place,” she explained. “I start by looking at what I'm making and working backward. What needs the oven? What needs the stove? What can stay in the refrigerator until the last minute? You don't want three dishes competing for the same burner when everyone's ready to eat.” She also recommends deciding how food will be presented before it is ready to leave the kitchen. Loading... You can use it for everything from searing chicken to sautéing vegetables or making a quick sauce, without having to pull out a different pan for every dish,” she says. “A little organization and the right tools can make the whole evening feel easier.” For those entertaining in an apartment or smaller home, Guarnaschelli suggests spreading refreshments across different areas to prevent guests from gathering around the stove. “The trick to entertaining in a small space is to give people a reason to spread out. If you put the drinks, appetizers, and main course all next to the stove, you're going to end up with a crowd exactly where you’re cooking!” A side table can become a drink station, while appetizers can encourage guests to mingle elsewhere. “I would put drinks in the living room, maybe on a bar cart or even a cleared-off side table, and keep a few appetizers somewhere else. A cheese board is great because people can help themselves without needing you to do anything,” she explained. Guarnaschelli also recommends making use of vertical space when arranging the food. “I also love using different heights when setting out food. items.title: Housing Market Feels the Chill as Buyers Pull Back—but Sellers Are Not Panicking Yet
items.description: The national housing market is feeling the chill as high borrowing costs are forcing frustrated buyers to throw in the towel, yet sellers are largely digging in to wait out the slump. Two key metrics— price cuts and delistings —tell the story of American home sellers' resilience in the face of adversity this fall. Across the U.S., about 4.4% of active listings were pulled off the market in October, down from 4.6% a year ago, according to the latest Realtor.com® monthly housing market trends report released on Wednesday. On a monthly basis, the delisting rate has ticked up slightly from 4% in September, in line with typical seasonal trends, but no more than that, even with mortgage rates well exceeding 7% and buyer demand waning. According to Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel , delistings matter because they act as a canary in the coal mine. A jump in the delistings rate could be a sign of a housing market in distress. However, the October findings show that sellers are not ready to take their ball and go home yet. "Job relocations, family circumstances, and financial challenges are among the top reasons I am seeing sellers stay on the market rather than withdraw and wait until spring," Josh Stimpson , a real estate agent at The Realtive Group of Reliant Realty in Nashville, TN, tells Realtor.com. "The rising cost of living is also a major factor, prompting many sellers to seek more affordable housing." Price cuts plateau The other key data point used to assess the strength of the U.S. housing market is price cuts. According to the latest housing market data, much like with delistings, there has not been a dramatic change up or down in the share of listings offering discounts, although it remained elevated. For the fourth consecutive month, more than 1 in 5 active listings (20.5%) saw a price cut, marking the highest October reading since 2022 and the second highest this year, trailing only September, which set a four-year record. However, Krimmel points out that the national price cut rate actually retreated 0.3 percentage points month over month, snapping a nine-month streak of monthly gains. Annually, the share of active listings with price cuts ticked up by just 0.2 percentage points. Sellers "are getting used to not everything selling quickly," Learka Bosnak , an agent with of Heather & Learka Team at Douglas Elliman in Beverly Hills, CA , tells Realtor.com. "They aren’t seeing compelling evidence that a slightly lower price will lead to a quick sale. Plus, they aren't feeling a lot of pressure monthly because so many have low-interest-rate mortgages." Loading... A pause, not a panic Taken together, the October delisting and price cut readouts lead to one conclusion concerning the present state of the market. "Right now, it looks more like a seller pause than an exodus," says Krimmel. "Sellers are disengaging rather than showing signs of distress." Regionally, price reductions remained least common in the systemically undersupplied Northeast (16.8% of listings) and most common in the West (21.9%), with the Midwest and South falling in between at 21% each. Across the 50 largest metro markets, 12 saw price cuts on a quarter or more of the listings, unchanged from September. Thirty-four of the metros are running above their year-ago cut rate, down from 36 in September. At the local level, price discounts in October were most common in Indianapolis (31.8%), Denver (31.3%), and Portland, OR (31.1%). While the delisting and price cut numbers stop short of signaling a panic among sellers, October trends do point to a noticeable pullback. New listings and pending sales slump New listings—a measure of homeowners putting their properties on the market—dropped 9.5% from September and 7.5% from a year ago, marking the steepest decline in more than three years. "Sellers know this is a poor time to list, and you do not list into weak demand unless you need to," notes Krimmel. At the same time, pending sales plunged 10.5% year over year—the biggest annual drop since October 2023. However, active listings jumped 7.4% year over year, topping 1.18 million homes for sale—the fourth consecutive month of accelerated growth. This reflects properties piling up on the market as buyers see their purchasing power diminished by surging 30-year mortgage rates, which averaged 7.33% in October. For context, that is a staggering 107 basis points above October 2025 levels and 53 basis points higher than at the start of September. "Elevated interest rates and ongoing affordability challenges have caused many buyers to pause, and the midterm election may be adding to that hesitation," notes Stimpson. "As a result, showing activity has declined and days on market are rising, particularly in Nashville and the surrounding areas." Silver lining for buyers However, patient buyers willing to stick it out can still find attractive deals and see their negotiating position strengthened. "Buyers can often retain their inspection, appraisal, and financing contingencies while also requesting additional repairs, a longer closing period, or a home warranty," says Stimpson. "Properties with extended market exposure may offer even greater leverage, including opportunities to negotiate a lower purchase price or secure seller concessions." Looking ahead to late fall and winter, the Nashville agent says there are some encouraging signs on the horizon, including gradually easing mortgage rates, closings holding steady in Middle Tennessee , and premium listings continuing to attract multiple offers. Yet, both Stimpson and Bosnak agree that what the market sorely lacks is a sense of certainty. "No one is sure what the market or the world will look like in a year, so it doesn’t feel weird to lean into that wait-and-see part of human nature," says the Beverly Hills agent. items.title: Amazon’s ‘Fallout’ Filmed Inside This Rare Norman Jaffe Estate—and It Was Just Listed for $4.25 Million
items.description: A stunning five-bedroom Long Island estate, designed by Norman Jaffe in 1977 and featured in the popular post-apocalyptic Amazon Prime series “Fallout,” has just hit the market for $4.25 million. Located in Old Westbury , the 5,291-square-foot home has a well-preserved midcentury modern interior, including a foyer with a 30-foot ceiling and an open floor plan with oversized windows, glass walls, stone and hardwood floors, pine ceilings, and three fireplaces. The sculptural structure has climbed its way to the top of the week’s most popular homes list . The inviting living room has a dual-sided fireplace and glass doors that open to the rear deck and pool grounds. The industrial-style kitchen has a center island, counter seating, and an eat-in area overlooking the pristine grounds. There is also a home theater for entertaining and relaxing. The 2.02-acre, resort-inspired lot is surrounded by mature landscaping and has expansive decks and patios with serene views. An in-ground pool with a spa and a two-car garage are also on the property. Other properties grabbing attention this week include Red Hot Chili Peppers founding member Flea ’s California compound, which is returning to the market with a price chop; a Tudor-style estate in Ohio ; and two lighthouses in Michigan offered for one low price. 10. 6830 133rd Ave SE, Lisbon, ND Price: $260,000 Why it’s here: This affordably priced, 1,800-square-foot “shouse” (shop/house) is designed for a collector, hobbyist, or outdoor enthusiast. The front of the engineered wood-frame building houses a one-bedroom residence, and the back has a two-car garage. Built in 2012, the building, known as The Roost, even has a cold equipment storage area. The home includes a living room, a kitchen with oak cabinetry, and a bathroom with a walk-in tub/shower. A walk-up loft over the living quarters could be used for extra storage or turned into an entertainment room. A covered patio overlooks the 3.2-acre lot and its wide open views.
